visual_spec.description: A coin flips ten times in slow motion, results appear one by one. A tally board shows 7H/3T. A slider labeled 'p' from 0 to 1 appears; as it sweeps, a likelihood bar chart responds in real time, peaking near 0.7.

frames.narration_spoken: Ten coin flips gave us seven heads. Which value of p makes this outcome most likely?

steps.label: coin-flips
steps.description: A coin flips ten times in slow motion, each result (H or T) appears in sequence
steps.narration_spoken: A coin spins through the air... ten flips, and seven land heads.

steps.label: tally-board
steps.description: Tally marks appear on a chalkboard: 7 marks under H, 3 marks under T
steps.narration_spoken: Seven heads. Three tails. That is our entire dataset.

steps.label: slider-appears
steps.description: A horizontal slider labeled p appears below, ranging from 0 to 1, with tick marks
steps.narration_spoken: Somewhere between zero and one sits the true probability of heads. Where exactly?

steps.label: slider-sweep
steps.description: The slider sweeps from 0 to 1, a vertical likelihood bar chart responds in real time
steps.narration_spoken: Drag p across its range. The likelihood bar rises... peaks... then falls.

steps.label: peak-glow
steps.description: Slider stops at p=0.7, likelihood bar peaks and glows golden
steps.narration_spoken: The peak sits near zero point seven. Coincidence... or mathematics?

visual_spec.description: Twenty height measurements scatter on a number line. Three candidate bell curves appear one by one — wrong center, wrong width, then the perfect fit. Two labeled knobs (mu, sigma-squared) appear on the final curve.

frames.narration_spoken: Heights on a number line. Which bell curve fits them best? Two parameters decide everything.

steps.label: height-scatter
steps.description: Twenty height measurements scatter along a horizontal number line, clustering around 170
steps.narration_spoken: Twenty students measured their heights. The dots cluster on the number line.

steps.label: bad-curve-left
steps.description: A narrow bell curve centered at 150 appears, poorly fitting the data
steps.narration_spoken: First attempt. A bell curve at one fifty... way too far left.

steps.label: bad-curve-wide
steps.description: A wide bell curve centered at 170 but sigma=20 appears, too flat
steps.narration_spoken: Right center, but far too wide. What went wrong with the spread?

steps.label: perfect-curve
steps.description: The perfect bell curve snaps into place, hugging the data tightly, edges glow green
steps.narration_spoken: And there... the curve that hugs every data point. How did we find it?

steps.label: two-knobs
steps.description: Two labeled knobs appear: mu (center) and sigma-squared (spread), with arrows pointing to curve features
steps.narration_spoken: Two knobs control the shape. Mu shifts the center. Sigma squared sets the width.

visual_spec.description: Eight data points float in empty space. Three candidate distribution curves fade in with different colors. Vertical likelihood bars appear beside each. The best-fitting one glows and wins. Title 'Maximum Likelihood Estimation' appears.

frames.narration_spoken: MLE picks the parameters that make observed data most probable.

steps.label: floating-data
steps.description: Eight data points float in empty space, no axes, no model
steps.narration_spoken: Raw data points, floating free. No model, no structure, just numbers.

steps.label: three-candidates
steps.description: Three different distribution curves fade in, each a different color, overlaying the data
steps.narration_spoken: Three candidate distributions step forward. Each one claims to explain these points.

steps.label: compatibility-bars
steps.description: Vertical likelihood bars appear next to each distribution, showing relative data probability
steps.narration_spoken: Which model assigns the highest probability to the observed data? That is the core question.

steps.label: winner-highlights
steps.description: The best-fitting distribution glows and the others fade, its likelihood bar is tallest
steps.narration_spoken: The winner has the tallest likelihood bar. It makes our data most probable.

steps.label: mle-title
steps.description: Text 'Maximum Likelihood Estimation' appears with a golden underline
steps.narration_spoken: This search for the best-fitting parameters... that is Maximum Likelihood Estimation.

visual_spec.description: A single coin splits into two paths (H/T). Probability labels appear. A compact formula P(x) = p^x (1-p)^(1-x) builds character by character. Verification: plug x=1 to get p, plug x=0 to get 1-p.

frames.narration_spoken: One formula encodes both heads and tails as a function of p.

steps.label: single-coin
steps.description: A single coin in the center, splitting into two paths: heads (left) and tails (right)
steps.narration_spoken: One coin. Two outcomes. This is the simplest random experiment.

steps.label: prob-labels
steps.description: Labels appear: P(heads) = p on the left path, P(tails) = 1-p on the right path
steps.narration_spoken: Heads happens with probability p. Tails with probability one minus p.

steps.label: compact-formula
steps.description: The formula P(x) = p^x * (1-p)^(1-x) builds character by character in the center
steps.narration_spoken: Why pack both outcomes into one formula? p to the x, times one minus p to the one minus x.

steps.label: plug-heads
steps.description: x=1 substituted, formula simplifies to p, arrows connecting to heads label
steps.narration_spoken: Plug in x equals one. The one minus x vanishes. You get p. Heads confirmed.

steps.label: plug-tails
steps.description: x=0 substituted, formula simplifies to 1-p, arrows connecting to tails label
steps.narration_spoken: Plug in x equals zero. The p to the x term vanishes. One minus p remains. See the power of one formula?

visual_spec.description: Ten coins in a row with outcomes. Multiplication signs connect individual P(xi) terms into a chain. The chain collapses into product notation, then simplifies to p^k * (1-p)^(n-k). Concrete values k=7, n=10 substitute in.

frames.narration_spoken: Independent trials multiply. The full likelihood is one compact product.

steps.label: ten-coins
steps.description: Ten coins in a row, each showing H or T, a bracket groups them together
steps.narration_spoken: Ten coins, each flip independent. The outcomes sit side by side.

steps.label: multiply-chain
steps.description: Below each coin, P(xi) appears, multiplication signs connect them into a chain
steps.narration_spoken: Independence means multiply. Each flip contributes its own probability factor.

steps.label: product-collapse
steps.description: The multiplication chain collapses into product notation, then groups like terms
steps.narration_spoken: What happens when we group like terms? All the p factors merge into one exponent.

steps.label: count-trick
steps.description: Exponents sum: p^k * (1-p)^(n-k) with k = sum(xi) highlighted in a box
steps.narration_spoken: p to the k, times one minus p to the n minus k. Why does counting heads simplify everything?

steps.label: concrete-numbers
steps.description: k=7, n=10 substituted, the expression glows with concrete values
steps.narration_spoken: For our coin... k equals seven, n equals ten. p to the seventh, times one minus p cubed.

visual_spec.description: Left: a vertical stack of 1000 tiny probabilities multiplied. A log symbol sweeps across, converting to sums. The Bernoulli log-likelihood formula builds. Right: side-by-side plots of L(p) and log L(p), both peaking at the same p.

frames.narration_spoken: Logarithms convert products into sums. Same peak, simpler algebra.

steps.label: tiny-products
steps.description: A vertical stack of 1000 small probabilities being multiplied, result shrinking toward zero
steps.narration_spoken: What happens when you multiply a thousand numbers less than one? The product races toward zero.

steps.label: log-rescue
steps.description: A large log symbol sweeps across the product, converting multiplication signs into plus signs
steps.narration_spoken: The logarithm saves the day. Products become sums. Tiny numbers become manageable negatives.

steps.label: bernoulli-log-L
steps.description: The Bernoulli log-likelihood formula builds: log L = k*log(p) + (n-k)*log(1-p)
steps.narration_spoken: Here is the Bernoulli log-likelihood. k times log p, plus n minus k times log one minus p.

steps.label: side-by-side
steps.description: Left panel: L(p) curve. Right panel: log L(p) curve. Both plotted against p from 0 to 1
steps.narration_spoken: Two curves share the same peak location. Can you spot it on both plots?

steps.label: same-peak-line
steps.description: A vertical dashed line drops from both peaks, showing they occur at the same p value
steps.narration_spoken: Both peak at exactly the same p. The log just turns multiplication into addition.

visual_spec.description: The derivative d/dp of log L is computed step by step. Two color-coded terms emerge: k/p and -(n-k)/(1-p). Set equal to zero. Cross-multiplication and algebra. Final result p-hat = k/n in a golden box.

frames.narration_spoken: Differentiate, set to zero, solve. Three steps to the Bernoulli MLE.

steps.label: derivative-setup
steps.description: d/dp of the log-likelihood expression appears, derivative notation highlighted in blue
steps.narration_spoken: Time to hunt the peak. Take the derivative of log L with respect to p.

steps.label: chain-rule-terms
steps.description: The derivative expands to k/p - (n-k)/(1-p), each term color-coded blue and red
steps.narration_spoken: Two terms emerge. k over p in blue... minus n minus k over one minus p in red.

steps.label: set-to-zero
steps.description: An equals sign and zero appear on the right, equation set equal to zero
steps.narration_spoken: Where does the slope vanish? Set this equal to zero. That is the peak.

steps.label: cross-multiply
steps.description: Step-by-step algebra: cross multiplication, collecting terms, simplifying
steps.narration_spoken: Cross multiply. Collect terms. Aswin, the algebra here is just two clean lines.

steps.label: p-hat-reveal
steps.description: p-hat = k/n = sum(xi)/n appears in a golden box, the final result
steps.narration_spoken: p hat equals k over n. Just the fraction of heads. Does that match your intuition?

visual_spec.description: A sequence of 12 coin flip results appears. Students count heads, apply p-hat = k/n. Answer reveals 9/12 = 0.75. A biased coin icon confirms the result.

frames.narration_spoken: Your turn. Compute the MLE from raw coin flip data.

steps.label: flip-sequence
steps.description: A sequence of 12 coin results appears: H H T H T H H H T H H H
steps.narration_spoken: Twelve coin flips on screen. Read the sequence carefully.

steps.label: count-heads
steps.description: The heads light up one by one as student counts
steps.narration_spoken: How many heads do you count? Take a moment.

steps.label: apply-formula
steps.description: p-hat = k/n template appears with blanks for k and n
steps.narration_spoken: Fill in the formula. p hat equals the number of heads divided by total flips.

steps.label: reveal-answer
steps.description: Answer fills in: 9/12 = 0.75, with a checkmark animation
steps.narration_spoken: Nine heads out of twelve. p hat equals zero point seven five. Makes sense?

steps.label: interpret-bias
steps.description: A biased coin icon tilts toward heads, p=0.75 label glows
steps.narration_spoken: This coin favors heads. The MLE captures the exact bias from the data.

interaction.prompt: Given 12 flips (H,H,T,H,T,H,H,H,T,H,H,H), compute p hat using the MLE formula.
interaction.if_correct: Nine heads out of twelve gives p hat of zero point seven five.
interaction.if_wrong: Count the heads again carefully. There are 9 heads in 12 flips.

visual_spec.description: Python code builds line by line: imports, p-grid via linspace, log-likelihood evaluation, matplotlib plot. The plot renders showing a smooth curve peaking at p=0.75, marked with a red dot and dashed line.

frames.narration_spoken: Python confirms the log-likelihood curve peaks exactly at p hat.

steps.label: imports
steps.description: Python code: import numpy as np, import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
steps.narration_spoken: Python time. NumPy for the math, Matplotlib for the plot.

steps.label: p-grid
steps.description: p = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 200) with a visual number line of dots
steps.narration_spoken: Two hundred p values from zero point zero one to zero point nine nine. Why not start at zero?

steps.label: log-L-compute
steps.description: log_L = 9*np.log(p) + 3*np.log(1-p) code highlighted and executed
steps.narration_spoken: Evaluate the log-likelihood at every grid point. Nine log p plus three log one minus p.

steps.label: plot-render
steps.description: A smooth curve renders on matplotlib axes, log L(p) vs p, clear single peak
steps.narration_spoken: The curve rises, peaks, and falls. Where does the maximum land?

steps.label: peak-marker
steps.description: A red dot marks the argmax, a dashed line drops to p=0.75 on the x-axis
steps.narration_spoken: The peak sits at zero point seven five. Exactly where our formula predicted.

visual_spec.description: The score function (derivative of log-likelihood) is defined. A tangent line slides along the log-likelihood curve, showing its slope. At the MLE the tangent goes flat. Left region shaded positive, right region negative. A compass needle analogy.

frames.narration_spoken: The score function points toward the maximum like a compass.

steps.label: score-def
steps.description: Text: Score S(p) = d/dp log L(p), definition highlighted
steps.narration_spoken: What is the score function? Simply the derivative of the log-likelihood.

steps.label: tangent-slider
steps.description: A tangent line slides along the log-likelihood curve, slope value displayed numerically
steps.narration_spoken: A tangent line slides along the curve. Its slope changes sign as it crosses the peak.

steps.label: flat-tangent
steps.description: At the MLE, tangent goes perfectly horizontal, 'slope = 0' label appears
steps.narration_spoken: Right at the MLE, the tangent goes flat. Slope equals zero. The critical point.

steps.label: pos-neg-regions
steps.description: Left region shaded green (positive score), right region shaded red (negative score)
steps.narration_spoken: Left of the MLE, the score is positive. Right, negative. What does that tell you?

steps.label: compass-needle
steps.description: A compass needle icon points toward the MLE from both sides of the curve
steps.narration_spoken: The score always points toward the maximum. A built-in compass for optimization.

visual_spec.description: The Gaussian PDF formula appears with labeled parts. Five data points appear on a number line with small Gaussian bumps. PDFs multiply into a joint likelihood. Exponentials merge. Two unknowns (mu, sigma-squared) are highlighted.

frames.narration_spoken: The Gaussian PDF hides two unknowns: mu and sigma squared.

steps.label: gaussian-pdf
steps.description: The Gaussian PDF formula with labeled normalization constant and exponential kernel
steps.narration_spoken: The Gaussian PDF. A normalization constant out front, an exponential decay inside.

steps.label: five-data-points
steps.description: Five data points appear on a number line, each with a small Gaussian bump at its location
steps.narration_spoken: Five observations arrive. Each one drawn independently from the same Gaussian.

steps.label: multiply-pdfs
steps.description: The five individual PDFs are multiplied together into a joint likelihood expression
steps.narration_spoken: What does independence give us? Multiply the five PDFs into one joint likelihood.

steps.label: exponential-merge
steps.description: The exponential terms combine into a single exp with sum of squared deviations
steps.narration_spoken: The exponentials merge. A single exponent holds the sum of squared deviations from mu.

steps.label: two-unknowns
steps.description: Mu and sigma-squared highlighted in red within the formula, arrows label them
steps.narration_spoken: Two unknowns hide in this expression. Mu and sigma squared. Can we find both?

visual_spec.description: Log applied to Gaussian likelihood. Three terms separate with line breaks, each color-coded: gray constant, red dispersion, green data-fit. The full expression is shown. Mu and sigma-squared glow as optimization targets.

frames.narration_spoken: The Gaussian log-likelihood splits into three color-coded terms.

steps.label: apply-log
steps.description: Log symbol applied to the Gaussian likelihood, transforming the product into a sum
steps.narration_spoken: Apply the logarithm. The product of exponentials becomes a sum of terms.

steps.label: three-terms
steps.description: Three terms separate with line breaks, each labeled: constant, dispersion, fit
steps.narration_spoken: How many terms emerge? Three, each with a distinct role.

steps.label: full-expression
steps.description: Complete Gaussian log-likelihood expression assembled with all three terms
steps.narration_spoken: Here is the full log-likelihood. Three terms, each pulling its weight.

steps.label: color-code
steps.description: First term turns gray (constant), second turns red (dispersion), third turns green (fit)
steps.narration_spoken: Which terms actually matter for optimization? Only the red and the green.

steps.label: optimization-target
steps.description: Mu and sigma-squared glow as optimization targets, upward arrow labeled 'maximize'
steps.narration_spoken: Our goal: find mu and sigma squared that push this expression to its peak.

visual_spec.description: Partial derivative with respect to mu is written. Constant and log-sigma terms strikethrough and fade. Chain rule applied to the sum. Score equation set to zero. Solution mu-hat = sample mean in golden box.

frames.narration_spoken: Partial derivative with respect to mu yields the sample mean.

steps.label: partial-mu
steps.description: Partial derivative of log L with respect to mu notation appears in blue
steps.narration_spoken: Start with mu. Write the partial derivative of log L with respect to mu.

steps.label: terms-vanish
steps.description: Constant term and log-sigma term fade out with strikethroughs, only sum term remains
steps.narration_spoken: Which terms contain mu? Only the sum term survives. Everything else vanishes.

steps.label: chain-rule
steps.description: Chain rule applied: derivative yields (1/sigma-sq) * sum(xi - mu)
steps.narration_spoken: Differentiate each squared term. The chain rule gives negative two times each x i minus mu.

steps.label: score-zero
steps.description: Set equal to zero: sum(xi - mu) = 0, the score equation for mu
steps.narration_spoken: What equation must mu satisfy? The sum of all x i minus mu equals zero.

steps.label: mu-hat-result
steps.description: Solve: mu-hat = (1/n) * sum(xi) = x-bar, appears in golden box
steps.narration_spoken: Solve for mu... mu hat equals one over n times the sum of all x i. The sample mean.

visual_spec.description: Five data points (2, 4, 6, 8, 10) on a number line. A summation scaffold fills in. Division by n=5. Answer: mu-hat = 6. A bell curve centered at 6 fades in to confirm.

frames.narration_spoken: Compute mu hat from five data points.

steps.label: data-display
steps.description: Five data points appear on a number line: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
steps.narration_spoken: Five data points: two, four, six, eight, ten. What is mu hat?

steps.label: sum-prompt
steps.description: A summation scaffold: _ + _ + _ + _ + _ = ?
steps.narration_spoken: Add them up first. Two plus four plus six plus eight plus ten.

steps.label: divide-prompt
steps.description: Sum = 30 fills in, then division by n = 5 scaffold appears
steps.narration_spoken: The sum is thirty. Divide by five... what do you get?

steps.label: answer-reveal
steps.description: mu-hat = 6 appears with checkmark, number 6 highlighted on the number line
steps.narration_spoken: Mu hat equals six. Right at the center of gravity of these five points.

steps.label: visual-bell
steps.description: A bell curve centered at 6 fades in, hugging the five data points
steps.narration_spoken: A Gaussian centered at six hugs the data tightest. Aswin, the mean was hiding in plain sight.

interaction.prompt: Given data points 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, compute mu hat.
interaction.if_correct: Mu hat is six. The sample mean centers the Gaussian perfectly.

visual_spec.description: Partial derivative with respect to sigma-squared. Constant drops out. Two surviving terms differentiated carefully. Set to zero and solve. Result: sigma-squared-hat = (1/n) * sum(xi - mu-hat)^2 in golden box.

frames.narration_spoken: Partial derivative with respect to sigma squared yields the sample variance.

steps.label: partial-sigma
steps.description: Partial derivative of log L with respect to sigma-squared notation appears
steps.narration_spoken: What about the second unknown? Take the partial with respect to sigma squared.

steps.label: surviving-terms
steps.description: Constant term fades out, two terms remain: the log-sigma and the sum term
steps.narration_spoken: The constant drops out again. Two terms survive... the log and the sum.

steps.label: differentiate
steps.description: Step-by-step differentiation: -n/(2 sigma-sq) + sum/(2 sigma^4)
steps.narration_spoken: Careful differentiation here. Negative n over two sigma squared from the log. Plus squared deviations over two sigma to the fourth.

steps.label: solve-algebra
steps.description: Set to zero, multiply through by 2 sigma^4, rearrange to isolate sigma-squared
steps.narration_spoken: Set to zero and isolate sigma squared. What falls out?

steps.label: sigma-hat-result
steps.description: sigma-squared-hat = (1/n) * sum(xi - mu-hat)^2 in golden box
steps.narration_spoken: The result: sigma squared hat. Sum each x i minus mu hat squared, then divide by n.

visual_spec.description: Two curves: concave (maximum) vs convex (minimum). Second derivative of Bernoulli log-L computed and shown always negative. Brief Gaussian Hessian display. Both log-likelihood surfaces shown as concave hills.

frames.narration_spoken: The second derivative confirms: our critical points are true maxima.

steps.label: max-or-min
steps.description: Two curves side by side: concave hill and convex valley, question mark between them
steps.narration_spoken: We found critical points. But are they maxima or minima?

steps.label: bernoulli-second
steps.description: Second derivative of Bernoulli log-L: -k/p^2 - (n-k)/(1-p)^2
steps.narration_spoken: For Bernoulli, take the second derivative. Negative k over p squared, minus n minus k over one minus p squared.

steps.label: always-negative
steps.description: Both terms shown negative for 0 < p < 1, red 'NEGATIVE' stamp appears
steps.narration_spoken: Both terms are negative for any p between zero and one. Maximum confirmed.

steps.label: gaussian-hessian
steps.description: Gaussian Hessian matrix diagonal entries shown, both negative
steps.narration_spoken: For the Gaussian, the second partials form a matrix. Both diagonal entries are negative.

steps.label: concavity-visual
steps.description: Both log-likelihood surfaces shown as concave hills with peaks clearly marked
steps.narration_spoken: Concave means maximum. Convex means minimum. Which shape do our log-likelihoods have?

visual_spec.description: Python code generates 100 samples from N(5,4). A Gaussian log-likelihood function is defined. Two plots: sweep mu (fixed sigma), sweep sigma-squared (fixed mu). Both peaks match analytical sample mean and sample variance.

frames.narration_spoken: Numerical plots confirm every analytical formula we derived.

steps.label: generate-data
steps.description: Python: np.random.normal(loc=5, scale=2, size=100), histogram of data shown
steps.narration_spoken: Can the code match the math? Generate one hundred samples from a known Gaussian.

steps.label: define-log-L
steps.description: def gaussian_log_L(data, mu, sigma_sq): function with the formula inside
steps.narration_spoken: Define the Gaussian log-likelihood as a Python function. Three inputs: data, mu, sigma squared.

steps.label: sweep-mu
steps.description: Plot of log L vs mu for fixed sigma, showing a clear peak near sample mean
steps.narration_spoken: Sweep mu from zero to ten, holding sigma fixed. The curve peaks sharply.

steps.label: sweep-sigma
steps.description: Plot of log L vs sigma-squared for fixed mu, showing a peak
steps.narration_spoken: Sweep sigma squared from one to eight. Where does the peak land?

steps.label: peaks-match
steps.description: Dashed lines from peaks to x-axis, compared with analytical values, labels match
steps.narration_spoken: Both peaks land on the sample mean and sample variance. Formula and code agree perfectly.

visual_spec.description: A new dataset of 50 exam scores appears. Student predicts peak location analytically, computes by hand, then runs plotting code to verify. Analytical and numerical peaks shown side by side, matching perfectly.

frames.narration_spoken: Predict the peak, then verify with code.

steps.label: new-dataset
steps.description: A dataset of 50 exam scores appears in a code cell, summary stats shown
steps.narration_spoken: New challenge, Aswin. Fifty exam scores loaded into a NumPy array.

steps.label: predict-peak
steps.description: Prompt text: 'Before running code, predict the peak location'
steps.narration_spoken: Before running any code... where should the log-likelihood peak?

steps.label: hand-calc
steps.description: Scaffold for computing sample mean and sample variance by hand
steps.narration_spoken: Compute the sample mean and sample variance from the data. Write them down.

steps.label: run-verify
steps.description: Code runs, twin plots appear, peaks marked with red dots
steps.narration_spoken: Run the code. Do the numerical peaks match your hand calculations?

steps.label: match-confirmed
steps.description: Analytical values and numerical peaks shown side by side, matching, green checkmarks
steps.narration_spoken: A perfect match. Analytical and numerical MLE always agree for these distributions.

interaction.prompt: Given the exam score dataset, predict where the Gaussian log-likelihood will peak, then verify with code.
interaction.expected_answer: Peak at mu hat = sample mean and sigma squared hat = sample variance of the dataset
hints: Compute the mean of the data first
The variance is the average squared deviation from the mean
interaction.if_correct: The numerical peak matches your analytical prediction perfectly.
interaction.if_wrong: Recompute: mu hat is the mean, sigma squared hat is the average squared deviation from the mean.

visual_spec.description: Multiple MLE estimates from different samples shown as dots spread around the true value. The Cramer-Rao bound appears as a floor on estimator variance. Fisher information connected to the second derivative. MLE shown hitting the bound exactly.

frames.narration_spoken: The Cramer-Rao bound proves MLE extracts maximum information.

steps.label: mle-spread
steps.description: Ten different sample MLEs shown as dots on a number line, spread around the true parameter
steps.narration_spoken: Run the experiment ten times. Each sample gives a slightly different MLE. How precise are they?

steps.label: cramer-rao
steps.description: The Cramer-Rao inequality: Var(estimator) >= 1/I(theta), floor line drawn
steps.narration_spoken: The Cramer-Rao bound sets a floor on estimator variance. No unbiased estimator can go lower.

steps.label: fisher-info
steps.description: Fisher information I(theta) connected by arrow to the expected negative second derivative of log L
steps.narration_spoken: Fisher information powers this bound. It equals the expected negative second derivative of log L.

steps.label: mle-efficient
steps.description: MLE variance dot sitting exactly on the floor line, labeled 'efficient'
steps.narration_spoken: The MLE hits this floor exactly. It is an efficient estimator... the best you can get.

steps.label: info-extraction
steps.description: MLE shown extracting 100% of data information, other estimators extracting less
steps.narration_spoken: For Bernoulli and Gaussian, MLE extracts every drop of information. What more could you ask for?

visual_spec.description: Screen splits into two columns: Analytical (blue, left) and Numerical (orange, right). Each column fills with its respective steps. A neural network diagram shows where analytical fails. Both columns glow with complementary strengths.

frames.narration_spoken: Analytical MLE gives insight. Numerical MLE handles everything else.

steps.label: two-columns
steps.description: Screen splits: left column 'Analytical' in blue, right column 'Numerical' in orange
steps.narration_spoken: Two paths to the MLE. Analytical on the left, numerical on the right.

steps.label: analytical-steps
steps.description: Left column fills: derivative, set to zero, solve, closed-form result
steps.narration_spoken: The analytical path: differentiate, set to zero, solve with algebra. Familiar by now?

steps.label: numerical-steps
steps.description: Right column fills: grid search, evaluate, find max. Or gradient ascent loop.
steps.narration_spoken: The numerical path: evaluate log L on a dense grid, pick the highest point.

steps.label: when-analytical-fails
steps.description: A neural network diagram where the analytical column is crossed out, numerical glows
steps.narration_spoken: What if the derivative has no closed-form solution? Neural networks face exactly this problem.

steps.label: both-matter
steps.description: Both columns glow, text: 'Analytical = Insight, Numerical = Generality'
steps.narration_spoken: Analytical gives deep insight. Numerical handles any model. Master both.

visual_spec.description: Poisson PMF appears. Student writes the likelihood, takes the log, differentiates, solves for lambda-hat. Reveal: lambda-hat = sample mean, shown alongside mu-hat = sample mean with a 'same pattern' bracket.

frames.narration_spoken: Apply the MLE recipe to Poisson. Recognize the pattern.

steps.label: poisson-intro
steps.description: Poisson PMF displayed: P(x) = lambda^x * e^(-lambda) / x factorial
steps.narration_spoken: Surprise round, Aswin. A new distribution: Poisson with parameter lambda.

steps.label: write-likelihood
steps.description: Template for Poisson likelihood with blanks: L(lambda) = product of ...
steps.narration_spoken: Can you write the likelihood for n independent Poisson observations?

steps.label: log-and-diff
steps.description: Scaffolded steps: take log, differentiate with respect to lambda, set to zero
steps.narration_spoken: Take the log. Differentiate with respect to lambda. Set to zero.

steps.label: solve-lambda
steps.description: Blank for lambda-hat answer
steps.narration_spoken: Solve for lambda hat. What do you get?

steps.label: reveal-pattern
steps.description: lambda-hat = sample mean shown alongside mu-hat = sample mean, bracket labeled 'same pattern'
steps.narration_spoken: Lambda hat equals the sample mean. The same pattern as mu hat. The sample mean keeps winning.

interaction.prompt: Apply the MLE recipe to the Poisson distribution. What is lambda hat?
hints: The Poisson log-likelihood has a term: sum(xi) * log(lambda) - n * lambda
interaction.if_correct: Lambda hat is the sample mean. Same pattern as the Gaussian mu hat.
interaction.if_wrong: Derivative of Poisson log-likelihood: sum(xi) / lambda minus n. Set to zero and solve.

visual_spec.description: The coin from f01 and bell curve from f02 reappear with their MLE parameters. Two class Gaussians appear with a decision boundary. An arrow connects MLE to 'Naive Bayes Classifier' as the next lesson teaser.

frames.narration_spoken: These MLEs power parametric classifiers. That bridge awaits next lesson.

steps.label: hook-callback
steps.description: The coin from f01 and the bell curve from f02 reappear side by side
steps.narration_spoken: Where did this all begin? The coin and the bell curve.

steps.label: now-solved
steps.description: p-hat = 0.7 on the coin, mu-hat and sigma-squared-hat on the bell curve
steps.narration_spoken: Both now have optimal parameters. MLE gave us the best possible fit.

steps.label: two-class-gaussians
steps.description: Two Gaussians labeled Class A and Class B, each with their own MLE parameters
steps.narration_spoken: In parametric classification, each class gets its own Gaussian with its own MLE.

steps.label: decision-boundary
steps.description: The two Gaussians overlap, a vertical decision boundary appears at their crossing point
steps.narration_spoken: Where does one class end and another begin? Right where the two likelihoods cross.

steps.label: next-lesson-tease
steps.description: Text: 'Next: Naive Bayes Classifier' with an arrow from MLE to the classifier
steps.narration_spoken: Next lesson, these MLEs become the engine inside Naive Bayes. That bridge is waiting.

opening_hook: Seven heads in ten flips. Twenty heights on a number line. One question connects both: which parameters make this data most likely?
closing_summary: MLE for Bernoulli: p hat equals the fraction of successes, k over n
MLE for Gaussian: mu hat is the sample mean, sigma squared hat is the average squared deviation
Log-likelihood peaks confirm every analytical solution numerically
These estimators hit the Cramer-Rao bound and become the foundation for parametric classifiers
